name: Megalodon Ridge
approach: Start at the Bridge Creek Trailhead on Highway 20 near milepost 159, just over a mile east of Rainy Pass (paved lot on the north side of the highway at about 4,400 ft), where a short connector trail crosses the highway to the Pacific Crest Trail, and head south on the PCT. Follow the PCT roughly 9-10 miles, descending along Bridge Creek, to the junction with the North Fork Bridge Creek Trail near North Fork Camp. Continue on this increasingly brushy trail up the North Fork of Bridge Creek valley, crossing Grizzly Creek, to around trail-mile 14, where maintained tread effectively ends and you ford (or find a log crossing of) the North Fork of Bridge Creek - the crossing is easiest a few steps upstream at a cairn. From there it's off-trail travel: work up scree and third-class slabs on climber's right of the large waterfall draining toward Goode Glacier to avoid the worst of the brush, then commit to a steep, sustained bushwhack (roughly the last half-mile) through slide-alder and timber to gain the toe of the long East Ridge ("Megalodon Ridge"), which sits close beneath Goode Glacier's lower icefall. Total approach is on the order of 12+ miles with several thousand feet of gain before any roped climbing begins, so most parties treat this as a multi-day trip and bivy low on the ridge (water is reliable along Bridge Creek and its tributaries but scarce once you're up on the rock, so tank up before leaving the creek). Watch for hidden cliff bands in the brush, loose footing on the slabs beside the waterfall, and general route-finding difficulty in the alder - a faint boot-path or 'tunnel' through the brush, when found, saves considerable effort over thrashing blindly uphill.

approach_variants.name: Off the Bridge Creek trail to the toe of the arete descending northeast off the main ridge
approach_variants.notes:
From the Bridge Creek Trailhead on Highway 20 near milepost 159, just over a mile east of Rainy Pass at about 4,400 ft, head south on the Pacific Crest Trail roughly nine to ten miles down Bridge Creek to the North Fork Bridge Creek junction near North Fork Camp, then up the increasingly brushy North Fork trail.

Parties disagree on where to leave the trail. The first ascent left at an obvious clearing before Grizzly Creek and climbed from there to the toe of the arete. Others continue past Grizzly Creek to around trail-mile 14, ford the North Fork, work up scree and third-class slabs on climber's right of the large waterfall, and then commit to a steep sustained bushwhack through slide alder and timber for roughly the last half mile.

Either way the objective is the same feature and the total approach is on the order of twelve or more miles with several thousand feet of gain before any roped climbing. Most parties bivy low on the ridge; water is reliable along Bridge Creek and scarce once you are on the rock, so tank up before you leave the creek.

The first ascent climbed its first fifth-class pitch at dusk and bivied on a bench, with the real difficulty starting the next morning.
approach_variants.season: Late summer, August into September, once the approach bushwhack and the glacier are most passable; a long committing route that wants a stable weather window
hazards: Hidden cliff bands inside the brush and loose footing on the slabs beside the waterfall
A very long sustained ridge — 2,800 to 3,000 ft of climbing with about 5,000 ft of exposure on one side and 4,000 on the other
Mostly simul-climbed with sparse belayed pitches, so long sections carry limited protection
Very few documented repeats, so beta and bail options are both thin
Benightment on the ridge is a real risk, and the standard descent drops into the Park Creek drainage on the far side of the mountain
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The feature is a clean-looking arete that descends northeast off the main ridge, and you aim for its toe. Both ways of leaving the trail agree on that. It sits close beneath the Goode Glacier's lower icefall — near it, not on it.

The single strongest test is that you never cross the glacier. The Northeast Buttress, the peak's other big route on this side, is reached by stepping off the Goode Glacier across a moat at a band of red rock. This route is gained from the east, from brush and rock, with no glacier crossing at all. If you have crampons on to reach your base, you are on the Buttress.

The arete announces itself by being clean. It is described as a clean-looking arete precisely because the ground around it is not — the last half mile of approach is slide alder and timber. Emerging from brush onto a distinct clean crest running down to the northeast is the confirmation.

Count the first stage: simul-climbing up the lower arete to a tower at about 8,200 ft, then one rappel off it, and only then running-belay climbing along the crest toward the southeast peak. A rappel early on a ridge you are ascending is a strong positional marker and it is the first one this route gives you.

The crux is late and it is above the glacier: three long pitches of 5.9-5.10 on the southeast peak headwall, with easier options further left, and then an overhanging 5.10 headwall above the Goode Glacier near Black Tooth Notch with an icy moat to negotiate. If you have met your hardest climbing in the first half of the day, you are on something else.

descent_text: Descend the standard Mount Goode line: from the true summit, downclimb and traverse the connecting ridge/notch system toward Black Tooth Notch, the deep gap short of the summit block. This section is done in three single-rope rappels - the first drops fairly directly down the ridge crest, but the second and third are traversing rappels that trend skier's-right/rappeller's-left, so keep the rope's uphill end free and watch for pendulum swing. A 60m rope doing 30m rappels is standard; anchors along this stretch are mixed - some fixed tat/slings on horns and blocks, some natural gear anchors - so inspect any in-place webbing before trusting it. From Black Tooth Notch, three additional rappels (also ~30m on a 60m rope) drop more or less straight down the fall line of the Southwest Couloir; watch for tat marking the stations. That's six rappels total to get off the technical terrain. Once the couloir eases to class 3, if it cliffs out, move climber's left onto easier ground and then traverse back right into the basin beneath the gully; cairns and a climber's path lead down and out (looker's right) to the Park Creek Trail. Because the standard descent drops into the Park Creek/Stehekin drainage - the opposite side of the mountain from the Bridge Creek approach used to reach Megalodon Ridge - getting back to a car at the Bridge Creek Trailhead is a long second act: parties either arrange a shuttle or hike out via Park Creek Trail and Thunder Creek Trail to the North Cascades Highway at Colonial Creek (or, less commonly, loop back over to Bridge Creek/PCT), adding on the order of 15-20 additional trail miles beyond the descent proper. Loose rock in the couloir, rockfall risk from parties above, and aging/sun-bleached fixed webbing at some stations are the main descent-specific hazards.
